title: A durable bidirectional neural interface for movement and sensation

concept.text: Proposed innovation: a neural interface that reads a person’s intended movements, uses those signals to control their body or an assistive device, and returns useful sensory information through a neural feedback channel. Its defining capability would be the sustained integration of movement control and sensation: the user could act and receive information about the action’s effects within a dependable feedback loop.

Conceptual scope: durability means preserving useful function during prolonged, repeated use, rather than demonstrating movement decoding or sensory stimulation in an isolated session. Recording, decoding, movement actuation, sensory encoding and stimulation would need to work together with acceptable safety and practical operating demands. The proposal does not require recording every neuron, restoring every natural sensation or repairing the underlying injury.

significance.text: Conditional significance: a dependable combination of intended movement and useful sensory feedback could give people with severe paralysis more natural control of their bodies or assistive devices. Feedback could help users judge the consequences of an action and make corrections, potentially reducing reliance on watching every movement. These are anticipated benefits of the proposed capability; their magnitude and clinical value would require direct demonstration.

The revolutionary advance would be a reliable, usable movement-and-sensation loop that supports everyday activity over time. If it improved independence, reduced assistance or made meaningful tasks easier, it could change the practical consequences of paralysis for some users. Broader deployment would also depend on surgical burden, maintenance, training, accessibility and the range of people who could benefit. A compelling laboratory demonstration alone would not establish those outcomes.

Limits on the analogy and downstream impact: an engineered feedback channel need not reproduce the richness of an intact nervous system to be useful, but distinguishable stimulation is not automatically natural or functionally helpful sensation. An interface may bridge disrupted pathways without biologically healing them. Memory restoration and broader human–AI integration would require separate advances; neither follows from successful movement control with sensory feedback.

missing_breakthrough.text: Proposed capability gap: the missing advance is sustained, integrated performance across neural recording, movement decoding, precise stimulation, useful sensory coding and practical operation. Success in any one component would not establish the complete interface. The engineering challenge is to preserve the usefulness of the whole loop as the user, recorded signals and implanted system change over time.

Engineering synthesis: concrete barriers include maintaining usable recordings, keeping stimulation sufficiently selective, translating device or body state into feedback the user can interpret, and managing interference between recording and stimulation. Long-term implantation must also be evaluated for tissue effects and device failure. Practical wireless operation introduces additional demands for power, communication reliability and manageable equipment. These are proposed engineering considerations, not requirements verified by the retained scientific source.

Scope clarification: recording millions of neurons with no foreign-body response is a speculative engineering specification, not an established prerequisite for this innovation. The necessary recording scale, acceptable tissue response and stimulation precision should be determined by functional benefit and safety evidence. The supplied materials do not establish a numerical channel requirement, a validated biological-response threshold or a particular architecture that would be sufficient.

current_state.text: The supplied research attributes a 2023 result to Lorach and colleagues in “Walking naturally after spinal cord injury using a brain–spine interface.” It describes one person with chronic spinal cord injury whose decoded cortical activity controlled spinal stimulation for standing and walking. This remains a dated report attributed by the supplied research: the retained source material available to the review did not permit verification of the paper’s identity, participant count, injury history, control method or walking outcome.

The source-access limitation is material. According to the supplied review, the retained HTML contained only a cookie-access notice, with no inspectable abstract or article text. The earlier assertion that the result rested on an indexed abstract therefore cannot be sustained from these materials. Although the source index records a saved artifact, that does not establish that scientific content was successfully retained. This evidence gap does not show that the attributed result is false.

Conditional interpretation of the attributed result: if verified as described, a one-person brain–spine demonstration would support the feasibility of a neural bridge for movement. It would not, by itself, establish the proposed integrated sensory-feedback capability, generalization across causes of paralysis, broad independent use or deployment at scale. No inspectable scientific findings in the supplied record establish completion of the durable bidirectional interface.

Coverage limitation: the supplied review reports no bounded freshness-search record establishing developments through 2026-11-01. The materials therefore cannot support a comprehensive account of the field at that date or resolve whether subsequent work materially changed its position. Missing coverage does not contradict the attributed 2023 report.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration framework: multicenter studies should show sustained, independent use for varied everyday movement tasks with useful, distinguishable sensory feedback. Studies should include people with different causes of paralysis and report outcomes by participant and clinical context, so that success in a narrow group is not mistaken for broad applicability. These are proposed criteria, not established consensus standards.
completion_criteria.label: Multicenter sustained independent everyday movement with useful distinguishable sensory feedback

completion_criteria.text: Proposed tests of sensory contribution: controlled comparisons should assess movement performance with and without informative feedback under otherwise comparable conditions. Evaluation should distinguish the ability to detect or discriminate stimulation from the ability to use it to improve an action. Appropriate measures could include task success, errors, assistance required, correction of unexpected disturbances and user effort. The protocol should specify meaningful benefits in advance rather than treating any measurable difference as sufficient.
completion_criteria.label: Informative sensory feedback improves movement performance by prespecified meaningful criteria

completion_criteria.text: Proposed durability and reproducibility tests: follow-up should establish how function and safety change over time, including interruptions, recalibration, training, maintenance and any repeat procedures. Reports should make clear which tasks users perform independently and what technical or caregiver support remains necessary. Replication across participants, centers and operators would provide stronger evidence than repeated success under one team’s supervision. Definitions of sustained use, useful feedback and acceptable risk should be set prospectively and justified for the intended application; the supplied materials establish no particular duration or numerical threshold.
completion_criteria.label: Longitudinal function, safety and support requirements are documented

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries: a convincing demonstration should identify supported movements, sensory channels, environments and patient groups, together with failure conditions and operational burdens. Finite testing would establish demonstrated breadth within those boundaries, not literal universality across all movements, sensations or forms of paralysis. Completion would not imply biological repair, restoration of every natural sensation or suitability for every patient.
completion_criteria.label: Demonstrated operating boundaries, failure conditions and operational burdens are identified

related_concepts.text: Roster-based comparison with NRL-07, “A dependable neural communication channel for profound paralysis”: both concepts concern dependable access to neural signals for people with severe motor impairment. NRL-07’s stated goal is communication; NRL-17’s is movement control coupled to sensory feedback. They could share interface and reliability advances, but success in communication would not establish effective movement-and-sensation control, or vice versa. Only the neighboring concept’s title was supplied, so its detailed design and evidence cannot be compared.

Roster-based comparison with NRL-05, “Regenerate a severely injured spinal cord with functional reconnection”: both could address consequences of spinal cord injury, but their central mechanisms differ. NRL-05 proposes biological reconnection; NRL-17 proposes an engineered interface that could bridge disrupted function. Either could potentially complement the other, but neither capability follows automatically from the other. NRL-06, “Replace lost brain tissue while preserving learned function,” likewise concerns biological replacement and preservation of function rather than the proposed interface loop.

Roster-based comparison with NRL-03, “Whole-brain, cellular-resolution recording during natural behavior,” and NRL-02, “A general predictive theory of neural circuit computation”: advances in recording or understanding neural computation could inform interface design. Their goals remain distinct. NRL-17 does not establish a need for whole-brain cellular recording or a general theory of neural computation; its proposed success is defined by useful, durable function within a specified application.

Roster-based comparison with NRL-08, “A visual-cortex prosthesis that restores useful, detailed sight”: both involve supplying useful information through neural stimulation, but NRL-08 targets visual perception, whereas NRL-17 couples feedback to movement control. NRL-16, “Biologically repair the injured visual pathway,” instead targets biological repair. Shared challenges in useful sensory coding do not make these interchangeable capabilities.

Roster-based comparison with NRL-04, “Read and selectively repair the physical traces of specific memories”: accessing movement-related signals and delivering sensory feedback would not establish access to specific memory traces or the ability to repair them. Memory restoration remains a separate capability. These comparisons preserve the roster entries as distinct proposals and do not infer their achievement or detailed requirements from their titles.

brief.title: Dependable movement control with a sense of touch
possible: People with severe paralysis could control their own limbs or an assistive device through intended movements and receive useful sensations in return. They could feel the effects of an action and adjust it, with the system remaining dependable through repeated everyday use.
why: Useful sensation could help people judge a grasp or correct a movement without watching every action. Making everyday tasks easier could increase independence and reduce the help some people with paralysis need.

sources.showed: Lorach and colleagues reported that brain signals controlled electrical stimulation of the spinal cord, helping a person with spinal cord injury stand and walk.
sources.cited_for: The work supports the feasibility of linking intended movement to spinal stimulation.
sources.not_established: Movement control alone does not establish useful sensory feedback or dependable everyday use.

sources.who: Santosh Chandrasekaran, Sarah K Wandelt and colleagues
sources.showed: A system linked intended hand movements with electrical stimulation and sensory feedback in a person with paralysis of all limbs. It enabled self-feeding and delicate object handling, alongside lasting gains in movement and touch.
sources.quote: this hybrid approach enabled recovery of functional abilities including self-feeding and manipulation of delicate objects, while also producing significant and persistent improvements in elbow flexion and wrist tactile sensation.
sources.cited_for: The work demonstrates movement and sensation together in the user's own hand.
sources.not_established: A single participant's results do not establish sustained independence across people, settings and clinical teams.

sources.showed: A person with paralysis of all limbs controlled a robotic arm through brain signals. Electrical stimulation of the brain produced touch sensations that halved the time needed for tested tasks.
sources.quote: trial times on a clinical upper-limb assessment were reduced by half
sources.cited_for: The work shows that artificial touch can improve movement performance.
sources.not_established: A single participant's laboratory performance does not establish durable, independent everyday use.

sources.who: Jeffrey Lim, Po T. Wang and colleagues
sources.showed: A participant without paralysis controlled a powered walking frame through brain signals and received artificial sensations from both legs. Electrical stimulation did not disrupt the system's reading of movement intentions.
sources.quote: Control experiments verified that decoding was not affected by stimulation artifacts.
sources.cited_for: The work demonstrates walking-device control alongside artificial leg sensations.
sources.not_established: The study does not establish benefit in people with paralysis or improved walking performance from sensory feedback.

shown: Chandrasekaran, Wandelt and colleagues combined control of a person's own hand with sensory feedback, enabling self-feeding and delicate object handling. The system's interpretation of movement intentions remained consistent over five months. This was a single participant.

Flesher and colleagues showed that artificial touch improved robotic-arm tasks. Lim, Wang and colleagues combined walking-device control with leg sensations in a participant without paralysis. These demonstrations establish parts of the movement-and-sensation loop.
missing: Studies across clinical centers have yet to establish sustained, independent everyday use in people with different causes of paralysis.
Long-term testing must establish safety, reliable function and manageable needs for training, maintenance and assistance.
The movements, sensations, environments and patient groups the complete system can reliably support remain to be established.

milestones.label: Independent everyday movement with useful sensation across clinical centers
milestones.explanation: Studies across clinical centers would have to show sustained independent use for varied everyday tasks, with distinguishable, useful sensations across causes of paralysis. This would establish how broadly the system helps.

milestones.label: Sensory feedback meaningfully improves movement
milestones.explanation: Controlled comparisons would have to show that informative feedback improves movement by meaningful criteria set beforehand. This would distinguish useful sensation from stimulation a person can merely detect.

milestones.label: Lasting function, safety and support needs are documented
milestones.explanation: Follow-up across participants, centers and operators would have to document function, safety, interruptions and support needs over time. This would establish whether dependable use extends beyond supervised demonstrations.

milestones.label: Operating limits, failures and practical burdens are established
milestones.explanation: Testing would have to identify supported movements, sensations, settings and patient groups, alongside failures and operating burdens. This would define where the system can be used dependably.

uncertain: How much sensory information and how precise a stimulation pattern are needed for useful everyday control?
What duration, benefit, tissue effects and maintenance burden would count as acceptable for the intended users?

page.title: Bidirectional brain–computer interfaces for movement and sensation
page.definition: An implanted brain–computer interface reads a person’s intended movement and uses it to move their own limb or an assistive device. As the movement takes place, neural stimulation lets the person feel contact with an object or sense where the limb is. An experimental system already gives a person with tetraplegia control and touch in their own hand, but a specialist team operates it. The goal is a combined system approved for repeated home use by people with paralysis.

goal.need: About 15.4 million people lived with spinal cord injury in 2021. In a survey, 48.7% of respondents with tetraplegia ranked regaining arm and hand function as the change that would most improve their quality of life. Watching a hand close gives limited information about its grip. Feeling contact as well as directing movement could help someone pick up a fragile object or feed themselves. For those who could benefit from an implant, using it at home depends on being able to start and operate it, with a trained caregiver if needed.

completion.title: FDA approves an implanted interface for movement control and neural sensory feedback during home use.
completion.criterion: FDA grants premarket approval for an implanted brain–computer interface whose labelled indication includes movement control together with sensory feedback delivered through neural stimulation during repeated home use by people with paralysis. The approval covers the combined system and its intended population and conditions of use. Device-specific benefit, risks and operating life are evaluated within that indication.
completion.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, Premarket Approval framework, applied to the combined home-use indication; implanted-BCI guidance issued on 20 May 2021.
completion.threshold_quote: sufficient valid scientific evidence to assure that the device is safe and effective for its intended use(s).
completion.basis: FDA’s published standard evaluates safety and effectiveness for the labelled intended use. The combined movement-and-sensation home-use indication defines the scope of this test. FDA’s BCI guidance recommends home evaluation and long-term follow-up; it supplies no universal lifespan or functional-performance cutoff.

milestones.title: A primate uses a brain-controlled actuator and cortical touch feedback to distinguish objects above chance.
milestones.criterion: A non-human primate uses motor-cortex activity to move an actuator among visually identical objects. Contact triggers stimulation of sensory cortex that encodes an object’s tactile properties. During brain control, the animal selects the target significantly more often than chance. Chance is one in three in the published three-object task.
milestones.set_by: Behavioural convention of discrimination above chance, operationalised in O’Doherty and colleagues’ peer-reviewed 2011 protocol. The published task used a cursor or virtual arm.
milestones.threshold_quote: but still significantly exceeded the 33% chance level.

milestones.title: FDA authorises first-in-human testing of an implanted bidirectional interface after nonclinical review.
milestones.criterion: FDA permits a first-in-human investigation under an Investigational Device Exemption that covers both brain-based movement control and neural sensory feedback. Device-specific nonclinical evidence supports starting the proposed study in light of its foreseeable risks, anticipated benefits and the importance of the knowledge to be gained.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, implanted-BCI guidance, Sections III(N) and III(O), and early-feasibility IDE guidance. The testing recommendations are device-specific.
milestones.threshold_quote: the sponsor must first submit an IDE application and obtain FDA approval.

milestones.title: A person with paralysis demonstrates combined movement control and neural feedback in a feasibility study.
milestones.criterion: In an authorised feasibility study, a participant with paralysis uses decoded brain activity to control the limb, robotic arm or walking exoskeleton under study and perceives neural stimulation conveying information about contact or movement during the same task. The study documents initial clinical safety for this combined use.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, early-feasibility IDE guidance. The sensorimotor task specifies proof of principle for the controlled limb or device.
milestones.threshold_quote: Early feasibility studies may be used to provide proof of principle and initial clinical safety data.

milestones.title: A clinical study assesses safety and effectiveness of the combined interface over at least one year.
milestones.criterion: Participants using the combined movement-control and sensory-feedback interface are followed for at least one year. The study reports long-term safety observations and assesses effectiveness for the intended function using the protocol’s endpoints. Follow-up can take place within a feasibility or pivotal investigation.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, implanted-BCI guidance, Section III(O)(2)(c)(iii), recommended duration of clinical follow-up.
milestones.threshold_quote: A long-term follow up period of at least 1 year is recommended

milestones.title: A pivotal investigation demonstrates the bidirectional interface’s clinical benefit and safety at home.
milestones.criterion: The final system achieves its prespecified primary safety and effectiveness criteria in the intended population and conditions of use, including home use. The investigation demonstrates clinical benefit with statistical support for the combined movement-and-sensation indication. The protocol sets sample size, endpoints and success bounds; FDA gives no common numerical values for this device category. Pivotal clinical evidence supports the subsequent marketing-approval review.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, pivotal-investigation guidance, Sections 6.2 and 7.1, together with the implanted-BCI guidance on home-use evaluation.
milestones.threshold_quote: Studies should be designed to show both clinical and statistical significance.

not_found: No FDA premarket approval for the combined movement-control and neural-sensory-feedback home-use indication was found.
No published pivotal result for that combined home-use indication was found.
FDA guidance, the IEEE roadmap and DARPA programme documents supplied no common numerical threshold for operating lifespan, task success or recalibration burden.
ClinicalTrials.gov records NCT03680872 and NCT01894802 opened without substantive study contents; their papers supplied the protocol context reported here.
No position opposing pursuit of combined movement control and neural sensory feedback for paralysis was found in the DARPA statements, IEEE roadmap or FDA implanted-interface guidance.

results.finding: One participant with tetraplegia maintained stable stimulation amplitude ranges over one year of brain–spine interface use.
results.detail: The latest quantified walking-decoder time point was 11 months after first activation. The report describes regular home use over 7 months.
results.quote: However, these ranges of stimulation amplitudes have remained stable over one year of use, and stimulation thresholds did not change over time.

results.finding: One participant with tetraplegia completed successful robotic-arm trials 51.2% faster with cortical touch feedback.
results.detail: The authors acknowledge ongoing Data Safety and Monitoring Board oversight. The paper reports functional performance outcomes and gives no adverse-event results.
results.quote: Times for successfully completed trials decreased by 51.2%, from a median of 20.9 s to 10.2 s, when tactile feedback was provided

results.finding: In a two-macaque study, monkey N selected the target on 50.37% of brain-controlled trials, significantly above chance.
results.detail: The Robotic arms case uses the virtual arm as a proxy. The study tested a computer cursor and a virtual arm.
results.quote: In Monkey N with 50-recorded neurons, performance dropped further (50.37 ± 3.74 % versus 91.45 ± 1.91%), but still significantly exceeded the 33% chance level.

results.finding: FDA initially authorised the bidirectional prosthetic-limb feasibility study for 1 year. The study enrolled five participants.
results.detail: The paper reports the decision in its study methods. It describes the evidence used to prepare the IDE without reproducing FDA’s review.
results.quote: Initial approval from the FDA was granted for 1 year but has been extended to 15 years.

results.finding: Five participants with spinal cord injury received cortical stimulation that evoked hand sensations, with zero safety-related explants in the first year.
results.detail: The explant endpoint measures initial implant safety. The paper’s stimulation analysis does not isolate safety during combined robotic-arm control and sensory feedback.
results.quote: The primary outcome measure for the clinical trial is the safety of the participants, specifically that the device does not need to be explanted due to a safety concern within the first year of implantation. This criterion was met for all participants.

results.finding: In five participants with spinal cord injury, cortical stimulation evoked hand sensations for up to 10 years.
results.detail: The efficacy analysis assessed detection thresholds, perceived location and quality, and electrode function. It did not assess longitudinal performance on a combined robotic-arm task.
results.quote: ICMS was both safe and effective for up to 10 years.

results.finding: One participant with spinal cord injury achieved 2.8 mm mean object deformation during robotic grasping with cortical grip-force feedback.
results.detail: The source is an IEEE conference proceedings contribution. The supplied record gives no peer-review status.
results.quote: In a compliant grasping task with the goal of grasping a delicate object without crushing it, objects were deformed on average only 2.8 mm with ICMS-based touch feedback compared to 8.7 mm without.

results.finding: One participant with cervical spinal cord injury identified stimulation-evoked finger sensations with 99.0% mean accuracy in blinded testing.
results.detail: Neural recordings served only to verify connections and monitor for unexpected signal artefacts during the reported experiments.
results.quote: The subject was highly consistent in his identification of the projected field, with a mean accuracy of 99.0% (i.e., 386 of390 trials correct, including 78 of 80 in a block with 7-digit conditions and a no-stimulation condition).

results.finding: One participant with cervical spinal cord injury had a 7.5% firmness discrimination error rate with biomimetic feedback during brain-controlled robotic grasping.

results.finding: Three participants with cervical spinal cord injury had generally stable stimulation-evoked hand sensation locations over 2–7 years.
results.detail: Repeated sensory mapping supplied the longitudinal data. The closed-loop robotic grasping experiment was a separate task in one participant.
results.quote: PFs remained stable over the testing period, which spanned ~2 years for participants C1 and P3 and ~7 years for participant P2.

results.finding: ReHAB obtained an FDA IDE for implanted intracortical and peripheral nerve electrodes in an own-arm and hand study with 1 participant.
results.detail: The paper cites prior nerve-cuff safety findings. It does not establish which nonclinical evidence the FDA reviewed or how it weighed foreseeable risks, anticipated benefits, and the importance of the knowledge to be gained.

results.finding: In 3 rhesus macaques, electrode impedance and voltage excursion stabilized after 10–12 weeks of chronic somatosensory microstimulation.
results.detail: The experiment tested the sensory stimulation component. The paper does not tie the results to the risk–benefit review of a proposed bidirectional robotic arm investigation.
results.quote: We show that impedance and voltage excursion both decay with time but stabilize after 10–12 weeks.

results.finding: USC reports an FDA IDE for a bidirectional walking exoskeleton after a 1-person feasibility demonstration.
results.detail: The release attributes the IDE in part to the human demonstration. It gives no trial enrollment count or details of the nonclinical review.
results.quote: The demonstration helped the researchers earn an Investigational Device Exemption from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, which allows them to test the device in a clinical trial for patients with paraplegia.

results.finding: One participant with cervical spinal cord injury achieved 85% correct responses to movement perturbations using a brain-controlled robotic arm and cortical stimulation feedback.

definition = "An implanted brain\u2013computer interface reads a person\u2019s intended movement and uses it to move their own limb or an assistive device. As the movement takes place, neural stimulation lets the person feel contact with an object or sense where the limb is. An experimental system already gives a person with tetraplegia control and touch in their own hand, but a specialist team operates it. The goal is a combined system approved for repeated home use by people with paralysis.". Reason: The definition leaves the source of the feedback implicit and gives readers no comparison between a working clinical prototype and the proposed home system.

goal.need = "About 15.4 million people lived with spinal cord injury in 2021. In a survey, 48.7% of respondents with tetraplegia ranked regaining arm and hand function as the change that would most improve their quality of life. Watching a hand close gives limited information about its grip. Feeling contact as well as directing movement could help someone pick up a fragile object or feed themselves. For those who could benefit from an implant, using it at home depends on being able to start and operate it, with a trained caregiver if needed.". Reason: The prevalence figure alone does not explain why touch matters for grasping, which activities people value, or what home use requires.

add statement by Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, Revolutionizing Prosthetics programme, 2016: "the goals of delivering near-natural motor control and sensation to users of prosthetics.". Reason: Revolutionizing Prosthetics explicitly connects the joint motor and sensory goal to an implanted brain interface for a robotic arm.

edit m1: title = "A primate uses a brain-controlled actuator and cortical touch feedback to distinguish objects above chance."; criterion = "A non-human primate uses motor-cortex activity to move an actuator among visually identical objects. Contact triggers stimulation of sensory cortex that encodes an object\u2019s tactile properties. During brain control, the animal selects the target significantly more often than chance. Chance is one in three in the published three-object task."; threshold_quote = "but still significantly exceeded the 33% chance level."; threshold_ref = 7; refs = [7]. Reason: The animal makes the discrimination, and its observed scores belong with the results rather than in the test.

edit m2: criterion = "FDA permits a first-in-human investigation under an Investigational Device Exemption that covers both brain-based movement control and neural sensory feedback. Device-specific nonclinical evidence supports starting the proposed study in light of its foreseeable risks, anticipated benefits and the importance of the knowledge to be gained."; threshold_quote = "the sponsor must first submit an IDE application and obtain FDA approval."; threshold_ref = 8; refs = [6, 8]. Reason: The revised criterion states which investigation FDA must permit and removes individual studies and publication dates from the authorisation test.

edit m3: criterion = "In an authorised feasibility study, a participant with paralysis uses decoded brain activity to control the limb, robotic arm or walking exoskeleton under study and perceives neural stimulation conveying information about contact or movement during the same task. The study documents initial clinical safety for this combined use."; set_by = "US Food and Drug Administration, early-feasibility IDE guidance. The sensorimotor task specifies proof of principle for the controlled limb or device."; threshold_quote = "Early feasibility studies may be used to provide proof of principle and initial clinical safety data."; threshold_ref = 8; refs = [8, 9, 10, 11]. Reason: The previous criterion mixed three study verdicts into the test and described early feasibility as establishing safety beyond the initial data FDA expects.

edit m4: title = "A clinical study assesses safety and effectiveness of the combined interface over at least one year."; criterion = "Participants using the combined movement-control and sensory-feedback interface are followed for at least one year. The study reports long-term safety observations and assesses effectiveness for the intended function using the protocol\u2019s endpoints. Follow-up can take place within a feasibility or pivotal investigation."; set_by = "US Food and Drug Administration, implanted-BCI guidance, Section III(O)(2)(c)(iii), recommended duration of clinical follow-up."; threshold_quote = "A long-term follow up period of at least 1 year is recommended"; threshold_ref = 6; refs = [6]. Reason: FDA recommends a duration for collecting safety and effectiveness data, while the original criterion treats that duration as a common pass threshold and includes case results.

add not found: "No position opposing pursuit of combined movement control and neural sensory feedback for paralysis was found in the DARPA statements, IEEE roadmap or FDA implanted-interface guidance.". Reason: The programme documents and guidance distinguish technical and clinical uncertainties from an institutional judgment against pursuing the goal.
remove statement 2. Reason: The IEEE passage sets a goal for autonomous closed-loop neural therapies generally and specifies neither voluntary limb control nor sensory feedback to the user.
remove statement 1. Reason: HAPTIX specifies motor signals from peripheral nerves or muscles and feedback through peripheral nerves in people with amputation.
